A  In a former warehouse on the edge of a large city, rows of lettuce, basil and kale grow on shelves stacked eight levels high. There is no soil and no sunlight. Instead, the plants' roots hang in trays through which a nutrient solution circulates, and each layer is lit by strips of light-emitting diodes, or LEDs, tuned to the wavelengths that plants use most efficiently. This is vertical farming, an approach to agriculture that its supporters believe could help feed growing urban populations while using far less land and water than conventional farms.

B  The basic idea is not entirely new. Growing plants in water rather than soil, a method called hydroponics, has been studied since the nineteenth century, and greenhouses have long been used to extend growing seasons. What makes modern vertical farms different is the degree of control they offer. Temperature, humidity, carbon dioxide levels and light are all managed by computer, often with the help of sensors that monitor every tray. Because conditions are identical throughout the year, crops can be harvested continuously, and some leafy vegetables can be grown from seed to harvest in less than a month.

C  The advantages claimed for this approach are considerable. Since water in a closed system is recycled, vertical farms can use as little as five per cent of the water needed to grow the same crop in a field. As the plants are grown indoors, there is little need for pesticides, and harvests are not affected by droughts, floods or frosts. Locating farms inside cities also means that produce can reach shops within hours of being picked, reducing transport and food waste. In places with little farmland or a harsh climate, such as some desert states and densely populated islands, these benefits are especially attractive.

D  However, vertical farming faces a major obstacle: energy. In a field, sunlight is free; in a vertical farm, every unit of light must be produced electrically, and the heat generated by lamps and equipment must be removed by air-conditioning systems. Electricity is often the largest single operating cost. Several well-funded vertical farming companies have closed in recent years after struggling to make a profit, particularly when energy prices rose sharply. Unless the electricity comes from renewable sources, the carbon footprint of indoor crops may also be higher than that of crops grown outdoors and transported over long distances.

E  For these reasons, the range of crops that can be grown profitably is still narrow. Leafy greens and herbs are well suited to vertical farms because they grow quickly, are compact and are almost entirely edible. Staple crops such as wheat, rice and maize, on the other hand, need a great deal of light and space, and they sell for low prices. Researchers have calculated that growing wheat indoors would be far too expensive to compete with conventional farming, at least with current technology.

F  Vertical farming is therefore unlikely to replace traditional agriculture. Its more realistic role may be to complement it, supplying fresh, high-value produce close to consumers and providing reliable harvests in regions where outdoor farming is difficult. Improvements in LED efficiency, cheaper renewable energy and plant varieties bred specifically for indoor conditions could all help to widen that role in the coming decades. Some companies are already experimenting with strawberries, tomatoes and even mushrooms, and a few farms are being built next to power stations or data centres so that waste heat can be put to use. Whether these experiments succeed will depend largely on cost.

Engineering Water in the Ancient World

A  Long before modern pumps and pipelines, people in many parts of the world developed remarkably sophisticated ways of finding, moving and storing water. These systems were not merely technical achievements; they shaped where cities could be built, how societies were organised and, in some cases, how long those societies survived. Several of them continue to function today, and engineers are increasingly studying them for lessons about living sustainably with limited water.

B  One of the most ingenious solutions is the qanat, which appears to have originated in what is now Iran at least two and a half thousand years ago. A qanat is a gently sloping underground tunnel that carries groundwater from an aquifer, often at the foot of mountains, to fields and settlements many kilometres away. Builders first dug a 'mother well' to locate the water, then excavated a line of vertical shafts, which provided ventilation and allowed soil to be removed as the tunnel was dug. Because the water flows by gravity and remains underground, very little is lost to evaporation, a crucial advantage in hot, dry climates. The technology spread widely across the Middle East, North Africa and Central Asia, and later to Spain and the Americas.

C  The Romans are famous for their aqueducts, but the arches that tourists photograph today represent only a small part of these systems. Most aqueduct channels ran at or below ground level, following the contours of the landscape so that water descended at a steady gradient, which in some cases was less than half a metre per kilometre. Achieving such precision over long distances required careful surveying with simple instruments. In the city of Rome itself, water from eleven aqueducts supplied public fountains, baths and the homes of the wealthy, and the constant flow was also used to flush sewers.

D  In South Asia, the stepwells of western India took a very different approach. The Gentle Push: Is Nudging Good Policy?

A  Since the late 2000s, the word 'nudge' has moved from the pages of behavioural economics into the offices of governments around the world. A nudge, in the sense popularised by a 2008 book written by an economist and a legal scholar, is any feature of the way choices are presented that alters people's behaviour in a predictable way without forbidding any options or significantly changing their economic incentives. Placing fruit at eye level in a school canteen is a nudge; banning sweets is not. The appeal of the idea to policymakers is obvious: nudges promise improvements in health, savings and environmental behaviour at very little cost.

B  The theory rests on decades of research showing that people do not always behave as the rational, fully informed decision-makers assumed by traditional economics. We are influenced by how options are framed, we tend to stick with whatever happens if we do nothing, and we give too much weight to the present compared with the future. The designers of forms, websites and buildings cannot avoid influencing these tendencies, since every layout presents some options more prominently than others. The authors therefore argued that this 'choice architecture' should be designed deliberately, to help people make the choices they themselves would make if they had more time, information and self-control.

C  The best-known success concerns pensions. When employees must actively sign up for a workplace pension scheme, many never get round to it, even when they say they want to save. When they are enrolled automatically and must actively choose to leave, participation rises dramatically. Several countries have built automatic enrolment into national policy, and millions of additional people now save for retirement as a result. In my view, this example shows nudging at its best: the change is transparent, anyone can opt out, and it helps people achieve a goal that most of them already hold.

D  Not every application is so convincing, however. Many early studies reported impressive effects from small changes, such as reworded letters encouraging people to pay taxes on time. More recent large-scale analyses suggest that the average effect of nudges is real but considerably smaller than those early results implied, partly because studies with striking results were more likely to be published. A nudge that works in one country or setting may also fail in another. Governments that expect nudges to solve major problems cheaply are therefore likely to be disappointed.

E  A more fundamental criticism is ethical. Living in the Shadow of Volcanoes

A  At first sight, it seems strange that millions of people choose to live on the slopes of active volcanoes. Eruptions can destroy villages, and even small events can cover farmland in ash. Yet some of the most densely populated rural areas in the world, such as parts of the Indonesian island of Java, lie close to volcanoes. One of the main reasons is the soil. Soils formed from volcanic material are among the most productive on Earth, and farmers have been drawn to them for thousands of years.

B  Soil scientists classify most of these soils as andisols. They cover only around one per cent of the planet's ice-free land, but they are estimated to support a far larger share of the world's population. Andisols develop from volcanic ash and other fragments thrown out during eruptions, known collectively as tephra. Because these particles are often fine and glassy, they break down relatively quickly when exposed to rain and air, releasing minerals such as potassium, calcium and magnesium that plants need to grow.

C  As the ash weathers, it forms unusual minerals that give andisols their distinctive properties. These soils tend to be light and loose, with a low density and a large amount of space between particles. As a result, they are easy to dig and allow roots to spread freely. They also hold large amounts of water while still draining well, so that crops are less likely to suffer during short dry periods and less likely to become waterlogged after heavy rain. In addition, andisols often accumulate large amounts of organic matter, which gives them a dark colour and further improves their fertility.

D  Volcanic soils are not perfect, however. The same minerals that give them their useful physical properties also bind tightly to phosphorus, one of the three main plant nutrients. Phosphorus that is added as fertiliser can become locked in the soil, where plant roots cannot easily reach it. Farmers on andisols may therefore need to apply more phosphate fertiliser than farmers elsewhere, or use methods such as adding organic matter to keep the nutrient available. Fresh ash can also be acidic or contain harmful substances, and newly deposited layers may take years to become productive.

E  The famous vineyards on the slopes of Mount Etna in Sicily and the fields around Vesuvius near Naples show how long people have valued volcanic land. Roman writers praised the fertility of the Campanian plain, the region surrounding Vesuvius, long before the eruption of 79 CE that buried Pompeii. Today, coffee, tea, vegetables and fruit are grown on volcanic soils from Central America to East Africa and Japan. In many of these regions, farmers have developed their own practices over generations, such as building terraces on steep slopes to prevent the loose soil from being washed away by heavy tropical rain.

F  For the communities who farm these areas, the benefits must be weighed against the danger. Improved monitoring of volcanoes, including measurements of ground movement and gas emissions, has made it possible to give earlier warnings of some eruptions, and evacuation plans have saved many lives. However, people are often reluctant to leave land that supports their families, and some return to their fields soon after an eruption. Understanding why people live with volcanic risk requires an understanding not only of geology but also of soil, economics and attachment to place.

Soils formed from volcanic material are among the most productive on Earth, and farmers have been drawn to them for thousands of years.

B  Soil scientists classify most of these soils as andisols. They cover only around one per cent of the planet's ice-free land, but they are estimated to support a far larger share of the world's population. Andisols develop from volcanic ash and other fragments thrown out during eruptions, known collectively as tephra. Because these particles are often fine and glassy, they break down relatively quickly when exposed to rain and air, releasing minerals such as potassium, calcium and magnesium that plants need to grow.

C  As the ash weathers, it forms unusual minerals that give andisols their distinctive properties. These soils tend to be light and loose, with a low density and a large amount of space between particles. As a result, they are easy to dig and allow roots to spread freely. They also hold large amounts of water while still draining well, so that crops are less likely to suffer during short dry periods and less likely to become waterlogged after heavy rain. In addition, andisols often accumulate large amounts of organic matter, which gives them a dark colour and further improves their fertility.

D  Volcanic soils are not perfect, however. The same minerals that give them their useful physical properties also bind tightly to phosphorus, one of the three main plant nutrients. Phosphorus that is added as fertiliser can become locked in the soil, where plant roots cannot easily reach it. Farmers on andisols may therefore need to apply more phosphate fertiliser than farmers elsewhere, or use methods such as adding organic matter to keep the nutrient available. Fresh ash can also be acidic or contain harmful substances, and newly deposited layers may take years to become productive.

Roman writers praised the fertility of the Campanian plain, the region surrounding Vesuvius, long before the eruption of 79 CE that buried Pompeii. Today, coffee, tea, vegetables and fruit are grown on volcanic soils from Central America to East Africa and Japan. In many of these regions, farmers have developed their own practices over generations, such as building terraces on steep slopes to prevent the loose soil from being washed away by heavy tropical rain.

F  For the communities who farm these areas, the benefits must be weighed against the danger. Improved monitoring of volcanoes, including measurements of ground movement and gas emissions, has made it possible to give earlier warnings of some eruptions, and evacuation plans have saved many lives. However, people are often reluctant to leave land that supports their families, and some return to their fields soon after an eruption.
